lessons.title: Solar resource and the photovoltaic effect

story.title: A rooftop in Jaipur at noon

scenes.text: A 1 m² panel in Jaipur receives about 1000 W of sunlight at noon on a clear day.
About 17–20 % of it is converted to electricity; the rest becomes heat.

steps.title: Solar resource
steps.body:
The **solar constant** is about 1361 W/m² outside the atmosphere (often quoted 1367). On the ground the clear-sky beam irradiance is typically up to ~ 1000 W/m². **Air mass AM = 1/cos θ_z** (θ_z = zenith angle); AM 1.5 (θ_z = 48.2°) is the reference spectrum. **Peak sun hours** = daily insolation (kWh/m²/day) ÷ 1 kW/m²; most of India gets 4–7 peak sun hours. Direct (beam), diffuse and reflected components; tilt ≈ latitude for annual maximum. **Standard Test Conditions (STC)**: 1000 W/m², cell 25 °C, AM 1.5.
**Photovoltaic effect**: a p–n junction in silicon (band gap 1.12 eV) absorbs photons with E ≥ E_g, creating electron–hole pairs that the built-in field separates, producing photocurrent I_L. Cell types: mono-Si (≈ 20–23 % module), poly-Si, thin film (CdTe, CIGS), and newer PERC/TOPCon/heterojunction; Shockley–Queisser limit ≈ 33 % for a single junction.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Zenith angle 48.2°: AM = 1/cos 48.2° = 1/0.667 = **1.50**.

**Example 2.** Insolation 5.5 kWh/m²/day ⇒ **5.5 peak sun hours**. A 1 kWp array in a system with performance ratio 0.75 yields 1 × 5.5 × 0.75 = **4.13 kWh/day**.

**Example 3.** Photon wavelength for Si band gap: λ = 1240/E_g(eV) nm = 1240/1.12 = **1107 nm** (longer wavelengths are not absorbed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting module efficiency as the 'sunlight to AC' efficiency (system losses: temperature, inverter, soiling).
- Mixing kW and kWh, or kWp and kW.
- Forgetting that STC rarely occurs in the field (cell temperature is usually 45–60 °C).

activity.prompt: Insolation is 5.5 kWh/m²/day and performance ratio 0.75. Daily energy from a 1 kWp array (kWh, 2 decimals)?

lessons.title: Lab: PV cell model and module I–V characteristic

story.title: The datasheet of a 275 W module

scenes.text: A datasheet lists Voc, Isc, Vmp, Imp and temperature coefficients.
These numbers define the whole I–V curve at STC.

steps.title: Single-diode model
steps.body: **I = I_L − I₀ [e^((V + I R_s)/(n V_T)) − 1] − (V + I R_s)/R_sh**, with V_T = kT/q = 25.7 mV at 25 °C. Open-circuit voltage **V_oc = n V_T ln(I_L/I₀ + 1)**; short-circuit current I_sc ≈ I_L (∝ irradiance). **Maximum power point (MPP)** at V_mp, I_mp. **Fill factor FF = V_mp I_mp/(V_oc I_sc)** (0.70–0.83). **Efficiency η = P_max/(G·A)**. Temperature: V_oc falls ≈ −0.3 %/°C (≈ −2.2 mV/°C per cell), I_sc rises ≈ +0.05 %/°C, P_max falls ≈ −0.35 to −0.45 %/°C. A 60-cell module has ≈ 36 V_oc; series cells add voltage, parallel add current. Bypass diodes (one per 20–24 cells) limit hot-spot and shading loss.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking P_max = V_oc × I_sc.
- Applying a temperature coefficient to ambient rather than cell temperature (NOCT ≈ 45 °C).
- Adding module voltages when connecting in parallel.

activity.prompt: A module has Vmp = 31 V and Imp = 8.9 A. Pmax in W (1 decimal)?

lessons.title: Lab: MPPT and DC–DC converters for PV

story.title: Why the inverter hunts for a voltage

scenes.text: As clouds move, the MPP of the array shifts.
A converter adjusts its duty ratio to keep the array at the MPP.

steps.title: MPPT techniques
steps.body: Because the MPP varies with irradiance and temperature, a **DC–DC converter** (boost/buck/buck-boost) under an MPPT algorithm sets the operating voltage. **Perturb & Observe (P&O)**: perturb V; if P rises keep the direction, else reverse; simple, oscillates around MPP and can mis-track under rapidly changing irradiance. **Incremental conductance (IncCond)**: at MPP **dI/dV = −I/V**; if dI/dV > −I/V move right, else left. **Fractional V_oc** (V_mp ≈ 0.76–0.8 V_oc), **fractional I_sc**, and hill climbing/ML methods; global MPPT for partial shading with multiple peaks. **Boost converter**: V_o/V_in = 1/(1 − D). **Buck**: D. Effective load seen by the PV: R_in = R_load (1 − D)² for a boost.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Boost: V_in = 31 V (MPP), V_out = 48 V battery ⇒ D = 1 − 31/48 = **0.354**.

**Example 2.** MPP at V = 31 V, I = 8.9 A ⇒ R_mpp = 3.48 Ω; a boost converter feeding R = 12 Ω presents R_in = 12 (1 − D)²; to present 3.48 Ω requires (1 − D)² = 0.29 ⇒ D = **0.46**.

**Example 3.** At the MPP, dI/dV = −I/V = −8.9/31 = **−0.287 S**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a P&O step so large that it oscillates strongly.
- Ignoring the converter losses (efficiency ≈ 97 %).
- Using a buck converter when the array voltage is below the battery voltage.

activity.prompt: Boost converter: PV at 31 V feeds a 48 V battery. Duty ratio D (3 decimals)?

lessons.title: Lab: Stand-alone and grid-connected PV system sizing

scenes.text: A remote school needs 5 kWh per day of electricity with one day of battery backup.
The designer sizes array, battery, charge controller and inverter.

steps.title: Sizing steps
steps.body: 1. **Load**: daily energy E_L (Wh/day) and peak power. 2. **Array**: P_array (kWp) = E_L/(PSH × PR); PR ≈ 0.65–0.8 (includes temperature, soiling, wiring, inverter, MPPT). 3. **Modules**: N = P_array/P_module; strings: N_s = V_dc/V_mp (series), N_p parallel; check the cold-temperature V_oc ≤ inverter max input voltage. 4. **Battery (off-grid)**: C(Ah) = E_L × days of autonomy/(DoD × η_batt × V_bus); DoD ≈ 0.5 (lead-acid), 0.8–0.9 (LFP Li-ion). 5. **Charge controller** (MPPT): I = P_array/V_bat × 1.25 safety. 6. **Inverter** ≥ 1.25 × peak AC load (surge for motors). 7. **Cables** ≤ 1–2 % drop; protection (DC fuses, SPD, DC isolator, earthing). **On-grid**: net metering, DC/AC ratio 1.1–1.3, string inverters/micro-inverters, anti-islanding.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** E_L = 5 kWh/day, PSH = 5, PR = 0.75 ⇒ P_array = 5/(5 × 0.75) = **1.333 kWp** ⇒ with 275 W modules N = 1333/275 = 4.85 ⇒ **5 modules**.

**Example 2.** Battery: autonomy 1 day, DoD 0.5, η = 0.9, 48 V: Wh = 5000/(0.5 × 0.9) = 11 111 Wh ⇒ Ah = 11 111/48 = **231.5 Ah** (choose 250 Ah).

**Example 3.** Charge controller current: 1375 W/48 V × 1.25 = **35.8 A** ⇒ 40 A MPPT controller.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring cold-weather V_oc rise (can exceed 1000 V or 1500 V limits).
- Taking DoD = 100 %.
- Oversizing the array without sizing the controller.

activity.prompt: Daily load 5 kWh, PSH 5, PR 0.75: array size in kWp (3 decimals)?

options: Exporting surplus to grid with credit

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — rooftop economics and LCOE

scenes.text: A factory plans a 100 kWp rooftop system and wants to know the cost per unit.
LCOE compares solar with grid tariff.

steps.title: LCOE
steps.body: **Levelised cost of energy** = (annualised capital + O&M)/(annual energy): LCOE = (I·CRF + O&M)/E_annual, where **CRF = r(1 + r)ⁿ/((1 + r)ⁿ − 1)**. Annual energy E = P × 8760 × CUF (capacity utilisation factor; solar in India ≈ 17–25 %). Payback = capex/(annual savings). Consider degradation (≈ 0.5 %/yr), inverter replacement and tariff escalation.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Capex ₹45 000 per kW, O&M ₹800 per kW-year, r = 10 %, n = 25 years ⇒ CRF = 0.1 × 1.1²⁵/(1.1²⁵ − 1) = 0.1102. Annual cost = 45 000 × 0.1102 + 800 = **₹5 758 per kW-year**; energy = 8760 × 0.20 = **1752 kWh/kW-year** ⇒ LCOE = ₹5 758/1752 = **₹3.29/kWh**. If the grid tariff is ₹8/kWh, annual saving per kW = 1752 × 8 − 800 = ₹13 216 ⇒ simple payback = 45 000/13 216 = **3.4 years**. (Illustrative numbers, not a quotation.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring O&M, degradation and discount rate.
- Mixing AC and DC capacities.
- Using peak-sun-hours instead of CUF without PR.

lessons.title: Solar thermal: flat-plate collectors and concentrating systems

scenes.text: A hostel in Pune heats 1000 litres of water daily with rooftop collectors.
A selective-coated absorber behind glass traps heat.

steps.title: Flat-plate collector (FPC)
steps.body:
Components: transparent cover (glass), absorber plate with selective coating, tubes, insulation, casing. **Useful heat Q_u = F_R A [G(τα) − U_L (T_i − T_a)]** (Hottel–Whillier–Bliss) ⇒ **efficiency η = F_R(τα) − F_R U_L (T_i − T_a)/G**. Typical F_R(τα) ≈ 0.7–0.8, F_R U_L ≈ 3–6 W/m²K. Stagnation temperature up to 150–200 °C. **ETC (evacuated tube)** collectors have lower U_L (≈ 1–2 W/m²K) for higher temperatures. Systems: thermosiphon (natural circulation) and forced circulation; storage tank sizing ≈ 50–75 L/m² collector area.
**Concentrating solar power (CSP)**: parabolic trough (concentration ratio ≈ 70–100, ≈ 400 °C), linear Fresnel, **solar tower** (heliostats, C ≈ 300–1500, 565 °C molten salt), parabolic dish (Stirling). **Concentration ratio C = A_aperture/A_receiver**. Thermal storage (molten salt 2–10 h) makes CSP dispatchable. Applications: water heating, drying, cooking (box/parabolic), desalination, process heat, solar chillers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F_R(τα) = 0.78, F_R U_L = 4.5 W/m²K, T_i − T_a = 30 K, G = 800 W/m²: η = 0.78 − 4.5 × 30/800 = 0.78 − 0.169 = **0.611** (61.1 %).

**Example 2.** For A = 2 m²: Q_u = 0.611 × 800 × 2 = **978 W**. Over 6 effective hours: ≈ 5.9 kWh ⇒ heats 100 L of water by 21.1 MJ/(100 kg × 4.186 kJ/kgK) = **50 K**.

**Example 3.** Trough: aperture width 5.77 m, receiver tube diameter 0.07 m ⇒ C = 5.77/(π × 0.07) = **26.2** (aperture over the tube's circumference, the usual area ratio); some texts quote the 1-D ratio 5.77/0.07 = 82.4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ambient minus inlet temperature (sign) in the efficiency equation.
- Applying FPC equations to concentrators.
- Ignoring heat losses from pipes and tanks (can be 20–30 %).

activity.prompt: F_R(τα) = 0.78, F_RU_L = 4.5 W/m²K, T_i − T_a = 30 K, G = 800 W/m². Collector efficiency (3 decimals)?

lessons.title: Lab: Wind power — Betz limit, C_p, tip-speed ratio

scenes.text: A 2 MW turbine's blades sweep an area bigger than a football field.
It can never extract more than 59.3 % of the wind's power.

steps.title: Wind energy
steps.body: Power in the wind **P_w = ½ ρ A v³** (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level, 15 °C; A = π R²). Extracted **P = ½ ρ A v³ C_p**; **Betz limit C_p,max = 16/27 = 0.593**; practical large turbines reach 0.45–0.50. **Tip-speed ratio λ = ω R/v** (optimum 6–8 for 3-blade lift machines; 1–2 for multi-blade pumps). Power curve: cut-in (3–4 m/s), rated (11–13 m/s), cut-out (≈ 25 m/s); above rated, **pitch control** limits power. Wind shear: v₂ = v₁ (h₂/h₁)^α, α ≈ 1/7 open terrain (0.14); height increases yield. Air density corrections for altitude and temperature.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting v³ (doubling speed raises power eight-fold).
- Using diameter instead of radius in A.
- Quoting C_p above 0.593.

activity.prompt: Turbine D = 80 m, ρ = 1.225, v = 12 m/s, C_p = 0.45. Output in MW (2 decimals)?

lessons.title: Lab: Wind turbine generators — SCIG, DFIG and PMSG with converter

scenes.text: A 2 MW turbine needs a generator that tolerates variable rotor speed.
Power electronics decouple the machine from the grid frequency.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Type 1**: fixed speed squirrel-cage induction generator (SCIG) directly on grid, soft starter and capacitor bank (needs reactive power), simple but no speed control. **Type 2**: wound-rotor with variable rotor resistance (≈ 10 % slip). **Type 3 – DFIG**: wound-rotor induction generator, stator direct to grid, rotor through a back-to-back converter rated about **|s_max| × P** (≈ 30 % for ± 30 % slip): reduced converter cost; super- and sub-synchronous operation; LVRT challenge (crowbar). **Type 4 – full-converter** (PMSG or EESG, geared or direct-drive) with converter rated at 100 %; full grid-code capability. Gearbox ratio: rotor 15 rpm to generator 1500 rpm ⇒ 1:100 (3-stage). Control: maximum power point tracking (λ_opt or power signal feedback), pitch, yaw, reactive power/voltage.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** DFIG, 2 MW, speed range ± 30 % ⇒ converter rating ≈ 0.3 × 2 = **0.6 MW**; PMSG needs 2 MW.

**Example 2.** DFIG at 6-pole 50 Hz: N_s = 1000 rpm; operating range 700–1300 rpm. At 1200 rpm: slip s = (1000 − 1200)/1000 = **−0.2** (super-synchronous) ⇒ rotor power flows to the grid: rotor power |s| P_stator = 0.2 P_stator is fed to the grid in addition to the stator power, so the total electrical output is about 1.2 P_stator.

**Example 3.** Gearbox ratio = 1500/15 = **100**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DFIG converter handles full power.
- Ignoring LVRT and reactive power duties in Type 1.
- Confusing sign of slip in super-synchronous operation.

activity.prompt: A 2 MW DFIG operates with slip range ±0.3. Approximate converter rating in MW?

lessons.title: Lab: Wind resource assessment — Weibull, Rayleigh and energy yield

scenes.text: An anemometer mast has logged a year of 10-minute wind speeds.
The engineer fits a Weibull distribution and computes expected energy.

steps.title: Statistics
steps.body: Weibull pdf f(v) = (k/c)(v/c)^(k−1) e^(−(v/c)^k); mean speed v̄ = c Γ(1 + 1/k); for **k = 2 (Rayleigh)**, v̄ = 0.886 c and mean power density **= ½ ρ (6/π) v̄³** = 1.17 ρ v̄³ (W/m²). **Capacity factor CF = annual energy/(P_rated × 8760)**. Typical Indian onshore CF ≈ 25–35 %. **Wind power class**: power density at 50 m (e.g., > 300 W/m² good). Array effects: wake losses ≈ 5–15 %; spacing 5–9 D downwind, 3–5 D crosswind. Availability ≈ 95–98 %.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Rayleigh mean speed 7 m/s, ρ = 1.225: power density = 0.5 × 1.225 × (6/π) × 343 = **401 W/m²**.

**Example 2.** A 2 MW turbine produces 6000 MWh/yr: CF = 6000/(2 × 8760) = **34.2 %**.

**Example 3.** Net energy after 10 % wake and 3 % availability losses from 6000 MWh gross: 6000 × 0.90 × 0.97 = **5238 MWh** (CF 29.9 %).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using average speed in P = ½ ρ A v̄³ (underestimates energy because of v³ nonlinearity).
- Ignoring wake and availability losses.
- Confusing CF with efficiency.

activity.prompt: A 2 MW turbine yields 6000 MWh per year. Capacity factor in % (1 decimal)?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — select a wind turbine and compute yield and revenue

scenes.text: A developer must choose between two 2 MW turbines with different rotors.
Yield, cost and LCOE decide.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1. Compute annual gross energy: E = Σ P(v) f(v) × 8760. 2. Subtract losses (wake, availability, electrical, curtailment). 3. Compute CF and LCOE with CRF. 4. Compare. **Specific power** = P_rated/A (W/m²): lower specific power (larger rotor) gives higher CF at low-wind sites.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Turbine A: 2 MW, D = 90 m ⇒ specific power = 2 × 10⁶/(π × 45²) = **314 W/m²**; Turbine B: 2 MW, D = 110 m ⇒ 2 × 10⁶/(π × 55²) = **210 W/m²**. At a 6.5 m/s site, B's CF is higher (e.g., 38 % vs 31 %): energy = 2 × 8760 × 0.38 = 6658 MWh vs 5431 MWh; if B costs ₹1 crore more and tariff ₹3.5/kWh: extra revenue per year = 1227 MWh × ₹3500 = **₹42.9 lakh** ⇒ payback of the extra rotor = 1 crore/42.9 lakh = **2.3 years**. (Illustrative.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Selecting turbines by rated power only.
- Ignoring the cost of larger rotors/towers.
- Using gross instead of net energy.

lessons.title: Hydro power: head, flow, turbines and pumped storage

scenes.text: A mountain stream falls 50 m through a penstock to a turbine.
Upstream, a pumped-storage plant stores energy as water in the reservoir.

steps.title: Hydro basics
steps.body: **Power P = ρ g Q H η** (W) with ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², Q (m³/s), H net head (m), η overall (turbine × generator ≈ 0.85–0.92). Plant types: **run-of-river**, **storage/reservoir**, **pumped-storage** (reversible pump-turbine, round-trip efficiency ≈ 70–80 %). In India, **small hydro** is ≤ 25 MW. **Turbine choice** by head: **Pelton** (impulse, high head > 300 m, low flow), **Francis** (reaction, medium head 30–500 m), **Kaplan/bulb** (low head < 60 m, high flow, adjustable blades). Components: intake, trash rack, penstock, surge tank (water-hammer relief), draft tube, governor, tailrace. **Capacity factor** for run-of-river 40–60 %. Environmental: sediment, fish passage, resettlement, GLOF risk in Himalayas.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Q = 10 m³/s, H = 50 m, η = 0.88: P = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 × 50 × 0.88 = **4.316 MW**.

**Example 2.** Pumped storage: V = 10⁶ m³, H = 300 m ⇒ stored potential energy = ρ g V H = 1000 × 9.81 × 10⁶ × 300 = 2.943 × 10¹² J = **817.5 MWh**; with turbine and generator efficiency 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 ⇒ **662 MWh** deliverable.

**Example 3.** Annual energy of a 4.3 MW plant at CF 50 %: 4.3 × 8760 × 0.5 = **18 834 MWh**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gross head instead of net head (friction/penstock losses).
- Using Q in L/s or head in feet without conversion.
- Selecting a Pelton for a low-head site.

lessons.title: Lab: Biomass, biogas and waste-to-energy

scenes.text: Dung from 25 cattle feeds a digester.
The gas runs a cooking line and a small genset.

steps.title: Bioenergy
steps.body: **Biomass** conversion: thermochemical (combustion, **gasification** with producer gas ≈ 4–6 MJ/Nm³, pyrolysis) and biochemical (**anaerobic digestion**, fermentation to ethanol). **Biogas** (50–65 % CH₄, 35–45 % CO₂; calorific value ≈ 20–25 MJ/m³). Digester types: floating-drum (KVIC), fixed-dome (Deenbandhu), plug-flow, CSTR. Stages: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, methanogenesis; mesophilic 30–40 °C, retention time 30–40 days, pH 6.8–7.4, C:N ≈ 20–30:1. Dung yield ≈ 0.03–0.04 m³ biogas per kg fresh cattle dung. **Waste-to-energy**: incineration, RDF; **bagasse cogeneration** in sugar mills; **biodiesel/ethanol blending**. Carbon-neutral cycle (biogenic CO₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 25 cows × 10 kg dung/day = 250 kg ⇒ biogas = 250 × 0.036 = **9 m³/day**; energy = 9 × 21.5 = 193.5 MJ/day = **53.8 kWh/day** thermal.

**Example 2.** If a gas engine generator (30 % efficient) uses it: 53.8 × 0.3 = **16.1 kWh/day** electrical.

**Example 3.** Digester volume = daily slurry volume × retention time: slurry 250 kg dung + 250 L water = 500 L/day ⇒ 0.5 m³ × 40 days = **20 m³** (+ gas holder).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming biogas is pure methane (CV 35.8 MJ/m³).
- Ignoring the digester temperature in winter (poor yield).
- Mixing fresh dung dry-matter percentages with total slurry volumes.

activity.prompt: Biogas plant: 250 kg dung/day, yield 0.036 m³ per kg, CV 21.5 MJ/m³. Thermal energy in kWh/day (1 decimal)?

lessons.title: Lab: Geothermal, tidal, wave and OTEC

story.title: Energy from the sea and the earth

scenes.text: A tidal barrage fills and empties a basin twice a day.
Geothermal wells in Puga (Ladakh) are being explored for power and heating.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Geothermal**: dry steam, flash steam, binary-cycle (ORC) plants; Carnot limit η = 1 − T_c/T_h, real 10–15 % for low-temperature resources. **Tidal**: *barrage* energy per tide **E = ½ ρ g A h²** (A basin area, h range); *tidal stream* **P = ½ ρ A v³ C_p** (ρ_sea ≈ 1025 kg/m³). **Wave**: power per metre of crest **P = ρ g² H_s² T_e/(64π)** ≈ 0.5 H_s² T_e kW/m. **OTEC**: closed/open cycle using ΔT ≈ 20–25 K between surface and 1000 m depth; Carnot efficiency ≈ ΔT/T_h ≈ 6–7 %, practical ≈ 3 %. Challenges: corrosion, marine growth, cost, environmental impact.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Barrage: A = 10 km² = 10⁷ m², h = 5 m: E = 0.5 × 1025 × 9.81 × 10⁷ × 25 = 1.257 × 10¹² J = **349 MWh per tide**.

**Example 2.** Tidal stream rotor D = 20 m (A = 314 m²), v = 2.5 m/s, C_p = 0.4: P = 0.5 × 1025 × 314.2 × 15.625 × 0.4 = **1.0 MW**.

**Example 3.** Wave: H_s = 2 m, T_e = 8 s ⇒ P = 1025 × 9.81² × 4 × 8/(64π) = **15.7 kW/m**.

**Example 4.** Geothermal 150 °C source, 30 °C sink: η_Carnot = 1 − 303/423 = **28.4 %** (real ≈ 10–12 %). OTEC: surface 26 °C, deep water 6 °C: η = 20/299 = **6.7 %**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Celsius in Carnot formula.
- Forgetting h² in barrage energy.
- Applying the wind Betz limit unmodified to tidal streams with blockage.

lessons.title: Lab: Fuel cells and green hydrogen

scenes.text: A fuel-cell bus quietly runs on compressed hydrogen and emits only water.

steps.title: Fuel cells and electrolysers
steps.body: **PEM fuel cell**: anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O. Reversible voltage E° = 1.229 V (ΔG = −237 kJ/mol, 25 °C, liquid water); thermo-neutral voltage 1.48 V (HHV, ΔH = −286 kJ/mol), 1.254 V (LHV, −242 kJ/mol). **Cell efficiency (HHV) = V_cell/1.48**; typical operating V = 0.6–0.75 V; stack is series-connected cells. Types: PEMFC (80 °C), AFC, PAFC (200 °C), MCFC (650 °C), SOFC (800 °C). **Electrolysers**: alkaline, PEM, SOEC: operating 1.7–2.0 V per cell; **efficiency (HHV) = 1.48/V_cell**. Hydrogen: HHV 39.4 kWh/kg (141.8 MJ/kg), LHV 33.3 kWh/kg (120 MJ/kg). Ideal electrolysis energy ≈ 39.4 kWh/kg; real systems ≈ 50–55 kWh/kg. **Green hydrogen** = renewable-powered electrolysis; India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) targets production growth and use in refineries, fertiliser and steel.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_cell = 0.7 V ⇒ η_HHV = 0.7/1.48 = **47.3 %**; η_LHV = 0.7/1.254 = **55.8 %**.

**Example 2.** Electrolyser at 1.8 V per cell: η_HHV = 1.48/1.8 = **82 %**; energy per kg = 2F V/(M) = 2 × 96 485 × 1.8 × (1000/2.016)/3.6 × 10⁶ = **47.9 kWh/kg** (ideal current efficiency).

**Example 3.** Fuel-cell bus: 1 kg H₂ at 50 % (LHV) system efficiency ⇒ 33.3 × 0.5 = **16.7 kWh** electricity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing HHV and LHV.
- Treating hydrogen as an energy source (it is a carrier).
- Forgetting compression, storage and distribution losses.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Hydrogen has a wide flammability range (4–75 % in air); ventilation, leak detection and no ignition sources.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — battery storage sizing, round-trip efficiency and cost per kWh throughput

scenes.text: A hospital wants a battery to cover the evening peak with solar energy.

steps.title: Storage metrics
steps.body: Technologies: lead-acid, Li-ion (NMC, LFP), flow (vanadium), NaS, pumped hydro, compressed air, flywheel, thermal, hydrogen. Metrics: **energy capacity (kWh)**, **power (kW)**, **DoD**, **round-trip efficiency (RTE)**, **cycle life**, **C-rate**. **Usable energy = capacity × DoD**; **energy out = energy in × RTE** over a full charge–discharge cycle. **Cost per kWh throughput ≈ capex/(cycles × DoD × capacity)** (storage cost only). Applications: peak shaving, arbitrage, frequency regulation, backup, renewable smoothing.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Battery: 100 kWh, DoD 90 %, 6000 cycles, capex ₹20 lakh: throughput = 6000 × 0.9 × 100 = 540 000 kWh ⇒ cost = 2 000 000/540 000 = **₹3.70/kWh** (excluding energy, O&M and losses). With RTE 90 %, each delivered kWh needs 1/0.9 = 1.11 kWh of charge: if solar energy costs ₹3.3/kWh, the delivered energy costs ≈ 3.3/0.9 + 3.70 = **₹7.4/kWh** (illustrative).
Sizing: evening load 40 kW × 4 h = 160 kWh; usable fraction 0.9, RTE 0.9 ⇒ battery = 160/0.9 = **178 kWh** (usable basis); charge energy = 160/0.9 = 178 kWh from solar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting nameplate kWh as usable kWh.
- Ignoring degradation (80 % of capacity at end of life).
- Forgetting power rating (kW) versus energy (kWh).

lessons.title: Grid-connected inverters and active/reactive power control

story.title: The solar farm that held the voltage

scenes.text: A 50 MW solar farm supports the grid voltage by injecting reactive power at dusk.
Modern inverters control P and Q independently.

steps.title: Power transfer and VSC control
steps.body: For a voltage-source inverter with output voltage V_i∠δ connected through reactance X to a grid V_g∠0: **P = V_i V_g sin δ / X**, **Q = V_g (V_i cos δ − V_g)/X**. Small angles: P is controlled by δ, Q by the magnitude difference V_i − V_g. **Grid-following** (current-controlled) inverters use a **PLL** (phase-locked loop) to track the grid angle, dq current control (i_d → P, i_q → Q), LCL filter (≈ −60 dB/dec above resonance, damp it), and DC-link voltage control. **Grid-forming** inverters set voltage and frequency (droop, virtual synchronous machine) and can operate in weak grids/islands. Reactive power capability (e.g., 0.95 leading/lagging), volt–var and volt–watt (Q(V), P(V)) functions, power curtailment, and **ramp-rate** limits are grid-code duties.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_i = 1.02 pu, V_g = 1.0 pu, X = 0.1 pu, δ = 5°: P = 1.02 × sin 5°/0.1 = 1.02 × 0.08716/0.1 = **0.889 pu**; Q = (1.02 cos 5° − 1)/0.1 = (1.01609 − 1)/0.1 = **0.161 pu** (inverter exports reactive power).

**Example 2.** DC-link voltage for a three-phase inverter on 400 V line (SPWM, m ≤ 1): V_dc ≥ V_LL/(0.612 m) = 400/0.612 = **654 V** (SVPWM: 400/0.707 = 566 V).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P = V²/X for transfer (sin δ is missing).
- Ignoring PLL instability in weak grids (short-circuit ratio < 3).
- Forgetting that the inverter current limit (≈ 1.1 pu) restricts fault contribution.

lessons.title: Lab: Grid codes, anti-islanding, harmonics and voltage rise

story.title: Why a hundred rooftop systems tripped together

scenes.text: On a hot afternoon, voltage on a long feeder rises as rooftop PV exports.
Inverters trip on over-voltage and the feeder collapses repeatedly.

steps.title: Interconnection requirements
steps.body: **Voltage rise** at the point of connection: **ΔV ≈ (R P + X Q)/V** (line-to-line V, three-phase P and Q; Q negative when absorbed). **Anti-islanding**: inverter must detect loss of grid and cease energising within about 2 s (IEEE 1547, IEC 62116); passive (over/under V/f, ROCOF, vector shift) and active methods (frequency shift, impedance injection). **Harmonics**: current THD ≤ 5 % (IEEE 1547/519-based) and individual limits; **DC injection** limits; **flicker**. **Fault ride-through (LVRT/HVRT)**: remain connected through defined voltage–time envelopes and inject reactive current to support voltage (national grid codes define the curves — follow the applicable CEA/CERC/utility code). Protection: sensitive reverse-power effects, sympathy trips, fuse–recloser coordination with DER fault contribution (≈ 1.1–1.2 pu). **Hosting capacity**: maximum DER the feeder can take without violating voltage, thermal or protection limits.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 11 kV feeder, R = 0.5 Ω, X = 0.3 Ω: PV injects P = 1 MW, Q = 0: ΔV = 0.5 × 10⁶/11 000 = **45.5 V** = 0.41 %. For 5 MW: **227 V** = 2.07 %.

**Example 2.** With Q = −0.3 MVAr (absorbing) at P = 1 MW: ΔV = (0.5 × 1 + 0.3 × (−0.3)) × 10⁶/11 000 = **37.3 V** — volt–var absorption reduces the rise.

**Example 3.** THD: fundamental 100 A, harmonics 3 A (5th) and 2 A (7th): THD = √(9 + 4)/100 = **3.6 %** < 5 % ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Neglecting X (for MV feeders X ≈ 0.3–0.5 R can be significant).
- Relying only on passive anti-islanding with balanced local load.
- Setting inverter trip thresholds tighter than the code allows (nuisance trips).

lessons.title: Lab: Microgrids, droop control and hybrid systems

story.title: The island that lost its grid

scenes.text: A village microgrid with solar, a diesel set and a battery islands itself when the grid fails.
Droop control shares load among sources without communication.

steps.title: Microgrid
steps.body: A microgrid is a group of loads and DERs with defined electrical boundaries that can operate **grid-connected or islanded**. Components: DERs (PV, wind, diesel, micro-hydro), storage, controllable loads, **microgrid controller**, point of common coupling (PCC) with static switch, protection. Control hierarchy: **primary** (droop, local), **secondary** (restore frequency/voltage), **tertiary** (economic dispatch). **Droop**: **f = f₀ − m_p (P − P₀)**, **V = V₀ − n_q (Q − Q₀)**; sources share active power inversely to their droop coefficients: **P₁/P₂ = m₂/m₁**. DC microgrids reduce conversion stages for PV/battery/LED loads. **Hybrid systems** combine renewable sources with diesel or battery to reduce fuel and ensure reliability; dump loads/curtailment manage surplus. Standards: IEEE 2030.7/2030.8 microgrid controllers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Droop: m = 0.01 Hz/kW: a 50 kW increase drops frequency by 0.5 Hz.

**Example 2.** DG1 m₁ = 0.01, DG2 m₂ = 0.02 Hz/kW; load 90 kW: P₁:P₂ = m₂:m₁ = 2:1 ⇒ **P₁ = 60 kW, P₂ = 30 kW**; common frequency drop = 0.01 × 60 = **0.6 Hz**.

**Example 3.** Diesel savings: a hybrid supplies 40 % of 100 MWh/yr by PV; diesel at 0.3 L/kWh ⇒ saves 0.4 × 100 000 × 0.3 = **12 000 L/yr**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Parallel operation without synchronising conditions (V, f, phase) at re-connection.
- Ignoring fault current limits of inverters in island mode (protection fails to trip).
- Under-sizing the battery for black-start and ride-through.

lessons.title: Lab: Frequency stability, inertia and the role of storage

scenes.text: In a system with high solar share, a 2 GW generator trip makes frequency fall faster.
A battery responds in milliseconds to arrest the fall.

steps.title: Inertia and RoCoF
steps.body: Swing equation: **2H/f₀ · df/dt = P_m − P_e = −ΔP (pu)** ⇒ **RoCoF = f₀ ΔP/(2 H)** (pu power on system base; H in seconds). Synchronous machines provide inertia; inverter-based resources (IBR) do not unless they provide **synthetic/virtual inertia** or **fast frequency response (FFR)**. Reserves: primary (governor, seconds), secondary (AGC, minutes), tertiary. **Frequency nadir** and settling; under-frequency load shedding (UFLS). Storage (BESS) offers FFR within 100–500 ms. India's grid frequency band 49.9–50.05 Hz (IEGC; check current code). **Forecasting** (solar/wind, day-ahead and intra-day) reduces reserves; **flexibility**: gas/hydro, DR, storage, interconnection, curtailment.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ΔP = 0.1 pu, H = 4 s, f₀ = 50 Hz: RoCoF = 50 × 0.1/(2 × 4) = **0.625 Hz/s**; the frequency reaches 49 Hz in about 1/0.625 = **1.6 s** if nothing arrests it.

**Example 2.** With half of conventional generation replaced by IBR, H falls to 2 s ⇒ RoCoF = **1.25 Hz/s**, doubling.

**Example 3.** Kinetic energy: S = 100 MVA, H = 5 s ⇒ E = H S = **500 MJ**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using H on machine base rather than system base for RoCoF.
- Assuming batteries instantly solve all stability issues (current-limited, need grid-forming for voltage).
- Ignoring that low inertia also affects protection (RoCoF relays).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — hosting capacity study for a rooftop-solar feeder

scenes.text: A DISCOM must decide how much rooftop solar a feeder can host.
The study checks voltage, thermal and protection limits.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1. Feeder data: 11 kV, R = 0.5 Ω, X = 0.3 Ω to the farthest bus, transformer 5 MVA, peak load 3 MW, minimum load 0.8 MW. 2. **Voltage limit**: ±6 % band (or code limit); at minimum load with PV at noon the rise = ΔV ≈ (R P_net + X Q_net)/V where P_net = P_load − P_PV (negative: export). 3. **Thermal limit**: reverse flow ≤ 5 MVA transformer rating × 0.9. 4. **Protection**: fault level and reverse-flow settings, anti-islanding. 5. Mitigation: volt–var, OLTC settings, reconductoring, batteries, curtailment.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Allow +3 % voltage rise (330 V on 11 kV). With unity power factor PV: ΔV = R P/V ⇒ the net export allowed by voltage is ΔV_limit × V/R = 330 × 11 000/0.5 = **7.26 MW** (voltage-limited). Thermal: 0.9 × 5 = 4.5 MW net export ⇒ PV allowed = 4.5 + 0.8 (min load) = **5.3 MW** (thermal-limited). Hosting capacity = min(7.26 + 0.8, 5.3) = **5.3 MW**. With volt–var (Q = −0.3 P) voltage limit rises but thermal still governs ⇒ use storage or upgrade the transformer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking only maximum-load conditions (the critical case is minimum load, maximum PV).
- Ignoring thermal reverse-flow ratings of transformers.
- Forgetting protection coordination.

lessons.title: Smart grid concept, architecture and Indian programmes

scenes.text: Power once flowed one way, from big plants to passive consumers.
Now rooftop solar, EVs and smart meters make flows and information two-way.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: A **smart grid** integrates electricity infrastructure with digital communication, sensing, control and analytics to improve reliability, efficiency, integration of DERs and consumer participation. **Drivers**: renewables and DER, EVs, ageing assets, AT&C losses, demand growth, outage cost, cyber-physical technology. **Architecture** (NIST conceptual model): seven domains — Bulk Generation, Transmission, Distribution, Customer, Markets, Operations, Service Providers — with electrical and secure communication flows. Layers: physical (power system), sensing/actuation, communications (HAN/NAN/FAN/WAN), data management, applications. **Benefits**: self-healing, peak reduction, loss reduction, DER hosting, consumer choice (TOU, prepaid), asset optimisation. **India**: National Smart Grid Mission (NSGM, 2015) and the **Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS, 2021)** supporting loss reduction, smart prepaid metering and feeder separation; smart-grid pilot projects (e.g., Puducherry, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka) — verify current status in official sources.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** AT&C loss = billing efficiency × collection efficiency: if billing efficiency = 88 % and collection efficiency = 95 %, AT&C = 1 − 0.88 × 0.95 = **16.4 %**.

**Example 2.** Peak shaving: system peak 100 MW; DR/EE reduces it by 5 % ⇒ **5 MW** of avoided peak capacity of avoided peak capacity that need not be built.

**Example 3.** Load factor = average/peak = 70/100 = **0.70**; flatter curves reduce cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a smart grid as just smart meters.
- Ignoring interoperability and cyber security in design.
- Confusing technical losses with AT&C losses (which include commercial losses).

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: Smart grid = power system + sensors + communication + software + people.

lessons.title: Lab: Smart metering (AMI), MDMS and time-of-day tariffs

scenes.text: A DISCOM installs one million smart meters reading every 15 minutes.

steps.title: AMI
steps.body: **Advanced Metering Infrastructure**: smart meter (bi-directional, interval data, remote connect/disconnect, tamper alerts, power-quality data) + **communication network** (RF mesh, cellular 4G/NB-IoT, PLC) + **head-end system (HES)** + **meter data management system (MDMS)** + billing/analytics. Protocol/standards: **DLMS/COSEM** (IEC 62056; in India IS 15959), IEC 62052/62053 accuracy, class 1.0 or 0.5S. Use cases: automatic billing, prepaid/postpaid, **TOU/TOD tariffs**, outage detection, theft detection, DR signals, LV network visibility, net-metering. Data: 15-min intervals = 96 reads/day; each read ≈ 100 B including overhead. Privacy and cyber security are essential.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1 million meters × 96 reads × 100 B = 9.6 × 10⁹ B = **9.6 GB/day** (≈ 3.5 TB/year raw).

**Example 2.** TOD tariff: peak ₹9/kWh (6–10 pm), off-peak ₹5 (11 pm–5 am), normal ₹7. A consumer shifts 2 kWh/day from peak to off-peak: savings = 2 × (9 − 5) = **₹8/day** = ₹240/month.

**Example 3.** Billing energy check: meter pulses 3200 imp/kWh; 1600 pulses in an hour ⇒ **0.5 kWh**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring communication coverage in basements/rural areas.
- No data validation, estimation and editing (VEE) rules in MDMS.
- Not protecting consumer data.

activity.prompt: 1 million smart meters read every 15 minutes at 100 bytes per read. Data volume in GB per day (1 decimal)?

lessons.title: Lab: Distribution automation — SCADA, FLISR, VVO/CVR and reliability indices

scenes.text: A tree falls on an 11 kV feeder; automated switches isolate the fault and restore most customers within a minute.
SAIDI and SAIFI improve.

steps.title: Distribution automation
steps.body: **SCADA** (supervisory control and data acquisition): RTUs/IEDs at substations, master station, HMI, protocols IEC 60870-5-104, DNP3, Modbus, IEC 61850 (substation automation, GOOSE, MMS). **ADMS** integrates SCADA, **DMS** (network analysis, switching), **OMS** (outage management), GIS. **FLISR** (fault location, isolation and service restoration): fault indicators → isolate faulted section via sectionalisers/RMUs → restore healthy sections via tie switches. **VVO/CVR**: coordinated control of OLTC, capacitors and regulators to flatten voltage; **CVR factor** = %ΔP/%ΔV (typically 0.5–1.0). **Reliability indices**: **SAIFI = Σ N_i/N_T** (interruptions per customer), **SAIDI = Σ r_i N_i/N_T** (minutes per customer), **CAIDI = SAIDI/SAIFI**; ASAI = 1 − SAIDI/(8760 × 60).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** N_T = 10 000. Outages: 2000 customers for 60 min, 500 for 120 min, 1000 for 30 min. SAIFI = 3500/10 000 = **0.35**; SAIDI = (2000 × 60 + 500 × 120 + 1000 × 30)/10 000 = 210 000/10 000 = **21 min**; CAIDI = 21/0.35 = **60 min**.

**Example 2.** With FLISR restoring the 2000-customer section in 5 min: SAIDI = (2000 × 5 + 500 × 120 + 1000 × 30)/10 000 = **10 min** — a 52 % improvement.

**Example 3.** CVR: demand 100 MW, voltage reduced 3 %, CVR factor 0.8 ⇒ ΔP = 2.4 % = **2.4 MW**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing SAIDI per interruption rather than per customer served.
- CVR below statutory voltage limits.
- Mixing sustained and momentary interruptions in index definitions.

lessons.title: Lab: Synchrophasors, PMUs and wide-area monitoring

scenes.text: PMUs across the country timestamp measurements with GPS to one microsecond.

steps.title: PMU and WAMS
steps.body: A **phasor measurement unit (PMU)** measures voltage/current phasors (magnitude and angle), frequency and ROCOF, time-stamped by GPS (UTC) at 25/50 frames per second for 50 Hz systems (IEEE C37.118.1/.2; IEC 61850-90-5). **PDC** (phasor data concentrator) aggregates data to the control centre: **WAMS** (wide-area monitoring system); **WAProtection and control** (adaptive islanding, oscillation damping, voltage stability). Accuracy metric: **Total Vector Error TVE = |X_est − X_true|/|X_true| × 100 %** (limit 1 % for steady state). Applications: state estimation, oscillation monitoring (0.1–2 Hz), event detection, angle stability, islanding detection, disturbance analysis. In India: Unified Real Time Dynamic State Measurement (URTDSM) project by POWERGRID with PMUs across the network (check current status).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** True phasor 1.000∠0°; PMU estimate 1.005∠0.3°: X_est = 1.004986 + j0.005262; error vector = 0.004986 + j0.005262 ⇒ |e| = 0.00725 ⇒ TVE = **0.725 %** (< 1 % ✔).

**Example 2.** Data rate: 50 fps × 100 B = 5 kB/s ⇒ per day 5000 × 86 400 = **432 MB/PMU/day**; 1000 PMUs ≈ **432 GB/day**.

**Example 3.** Time error of 10 µs at 50 Hz corresponds to a phase error 360° × 50 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = **0.18°** (so GPS sync accuracy of 1 µs gives 0.018°).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using SCADA 2–4 s data to see 1 Hz oscillations (aliasing).
- Ignoring GPS time-sync failures/spoofing.
- Overlooking PDC latency in control applications.

steps.title: Demand response and communications

lessons.title: Arc phenomenon: how an arc is formed and sustained

scenes.text: A lineman opens a loaded 11 kV isolator by mistake and a blinding arc roars across the gap.
The air between the contacts has become a conducting plasma at several thousand kelvin.

steps.title: Arc formation
steps.body:
When contacts part, the contact area and pressure fall, so the current density at the last contact point becomes very high and the metal heats and melts. Mechanisms that start the arc:
- **Field emission**: a high field (> ~10⁸ V/m) at the cathode pulls electrons out of the metal.
- **Thermionic emission**: the hot cathode spot emits electrons (Richardson law).
- **Ionisation by collision**: electrons accelerated by the field strike gas atoms and release more electrons (avalanche).
The arc is **sustained** by thermal ionisation (high gas temperature gives molecules enough kinetic energy to ionise on collision) plus thermionic emission and secondary emission from the cathode.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Contacts separate while carrying 2000 A and the arc voltage is 100 V. Arc power = V·I = 100 × 2000 = 200 kW. For 20 ms this deposits 200 000 × 0.02 = 4 kJ in the contact gap and gas.

**Example 2.** Arc voltage ≈ electrode drop (about 15–40 V) + E·l, where E is the voltage gradient along the column. If E = 1 kV/m, for l = 0.3 m the column drop is 300 V. Lengthening the arc raises arc voltage and pushes the current toward zero faster; this is the principle of high-resistance interruption.

steps.title: Arc properties
steps.body:
- Arc column: very high temperature (5 000–20 000 K) and low voltage gradient; a good conductor with a negative resistance (volt-ampere) characteristic: voltage falls as current rises.
- Arc voltage is nearly independent of current in a long arc, and in AC it is nearly square-wave in shape.
- Arc resistance falls with larger cross-section, shorter length, higher temperature and ionisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the arc is sustained by field emission; it is sustained by thermal ionisation and thermionic emission.
- Treating the arc as an ohmic resistor of constant value.
- Forgetting that in AC an arc extinguishes naturally at every current zero, but can restrike.

lessons.title: Arc interruption theories and methods

story.title: Why AC is easier than DC

scenes.text: An AC current passes through zero 100 times a second at 50 Hz.
A breaker designer waits for that zero to win the race against re-ignition.

steps.title: Two methods
steps.body:
**High-resistance interruption**: raise arc resistance by lengthening, cooling, splitting and constricting it so that the current is forced down. Used in DC breakers, LV AC breakers and air-break breakers.
**Low-resistance (current-zero) interruption**: the arc resistance stays low until current zero, then the dielectric strength of the gap is built up faster than the recovery voltage. Used in all HV AC breakers.

**Slepian's (ionic) theory**: at current zero, the arc is extinguished if the rate of deionisation of the gap exceeds the rate of ionisation; deionisation is increased by cooling, pressure and blast.
**Cassie / Mayr energy-balance theory**: arc is extinguished if the energy removed from the gap (heat, blast, conduction) exceeds the energy input from the recovery voltage and residual current; the gap passes through a thermal phase and then a dielectric phase.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Each current zero occurs every half cycle. At 50 Hz the interval is 1/100 = 10 ms, and the breaker has a few hundred microseconds around zero to build dielectric strength above the recovery voltage.

**Example 2.** Methods to deionise: (i) lengthen the arc using magnetic blowout; (ii) split with arc chutes (splitters); (iii) cool with oil which produces hydrogen; (iv) blast with compressed air or SF₆ gas; (v) raise gas pressure. Match the method: air-blast breakers use a high velocity blast, MOCBs use controlled oil flow in an explosion pot.

steps.title: Race in the gap
steps.body: After current zero two things compete: the **recovery voltage** that rises across the contacts, and the **dielectric strength** of the gap that rebuilds. If the strength curve stays above the voltage curve the arc is interrupted; if the voltage curve crosses the strength curve the gap breaks down again (**thermal re-ignition** within ~1 µs–1 ms, **dielectric re-strike** later).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying high-resistance interruption to HV AC breakers: they use current-zero interruption.
- Saying Slepian's theory involves energy; that is the Cassie–Mayr energy theory.
- Confusing the thermal phase (right after zero) with the dielectric phase (later).

lessons.title: Lab: Restriking voltage and RRRV

scenes.text: After clearing a fault, the line side voltage snaps back to system voltage.
The L and C of the network make it overshoot as a damped oscillation at a natural frequency.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
After the arc is quenched at current zero, the system inductance L (behind the breaker) and the stray capacitance C (breaker side) form a series L–C circuit that is suddenly connected to the source emf. At current zero the source emf is at its **peak Em**, so the recovery voltage v(t) across the breaker (= capacitor voltage) satisfies L C v'' + v = Em, v(0)=0, v'(0)=0 ⇒

**v(t) = Em (1 − cos ωn t)**, with **ωn = 1/√(LC)**, **fn = 1/(2π√(LC))**.

Peak = 2Em (undamped) at t = π/ωn. With damping the peak is k·Em where k (the amplitude factor) is about 1.4–1.6 (first pole to clear: 1.5 × phase voltage in a 3-phase ungrounded fault).
**RRRV** = dv/dt: maximum value = Em ωn (at t = π/2ωn); average over the first peak = 2Em ωn/π.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Em = 100 kV, L = 10 mH, C = 0.01 µF. ωn = 1/√(10⁻²·10⁻⁸) = 1/10⁻⁵ = 10⁵ rad/s ⇒ fn = 15.9 kHz. Max RRRV = Em ωn = 100 000 × 10⁵ = 10¹⁰ V/s = **10 kV/µs**. Peak = 200 kV at t = π/10⁵ = 31.4 µs.

**Example 2.** Parallel resistance across the contacts damps the oscillation; critical resistance R = ½√(L/C) = ½√(10⁻²/10⁻⁸) = ½ × 1000 = **500 Ω**. For R below this the transient is non-oscillatory, so there is no overshoot. (Shunt resistors are used in oil and air blast breakers.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the rms value in place of Em (peak) in v(t).
- Quoting average RRRV (2Emωn/π) when maximum RRRV (Emωn) is asked.
- Forgetting that the transient frequency depends only on L and C, not on Em.
- Mixing mH and µH or µF and nF.

lessons.title: Lab: Current chopping and capacitive switching

scenes.text: A vacuum breaker switches off a lightly loaded 6.6 kV motor and a winding fails days later.
The breaker forced current to zero before its natural zero: the stored energy in the inductance went into an overvoltage.

steps.title: Current chopping
steps.body:
**Current chopping** is the forced interruption of a small current before the natural current zero (typical of air-blast and vacuum breakers with strong deionisation). The magnetic energy ½ L i² in the inductance (a transformer or motor magnetising or starting inductance) transfers to the stray capacitance C:

½ L I² = ½ C V² ⇒ **V = I√(L/C)**

Overvoltage ratio V/Em can be several per unit. Remedies: surge arresters, RC snubbers, low-chop contact materials (CuCr, which has chopping current ~3–5 A) and parallel resistors.

**Capacitive current switching** (unloaded cable or capacitor banks, line charging): the breaker interrupts a leading current at its zero, when the system voltage is at its peak and the capacitor retains that charge. Half a cycle later the voltage across the breaker is up to **2Em**, and a restrike can build further overvoltages (up to 3Em or more). Remedy: restrike-free breakers (SF₆, vacuum), pre-insertion resistors, point-on-wave controllers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Chopped current I = 5 A, L = 10 mH, C = 0.01 µF. √(L/C) = √(10⁻²/10⁻⁸) = 1000 Ω ⇒ V = 5 × 1000 = **5 kV**. If the system is 11 kV (peak phase = 8.98 kV) the overvoltage is 0.56 pu — not dangerous here, but with I = 20 A it would be 20 kV (2.2 pu).

**Example 2.** A 33 kV unloaded cable is switched; peak phase voltage = 33√2/√3 = 26.94 kV. At the first restrike half a cycle later the breaker voltage = 2 × 26.94 = **53.9 kV**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing chopping (inductive load) with capacitive switching (leading current).
- Using rms rather than peak for the capacitor charge.
- Assuming SF₆ and vacuum breakers never create overvoltages; vacuum breakers do chop current, so snubbers are used for motors.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — breaker ratings and short-circuit duty

story.title: Selecting the breaker for a new 11 kV bus

scenes.text: A substation engineer must pick the breaker for an 11 kV bus fed by a 2000 MVA grid.
She converts MVA to kA, then adds making capacity and duty margins.

steps.title: Ratings
steps.body:
- **Rated voltage**: highest system voltage (e.g. 12 kV for 11 kV system).
- **Rated normal current**: continuous current without exceeding temperature rise.
- **Rated short-circuit breaking current** (rms of AC component at contact separation): symmetrical breaking current Isym; **breaking capacity (MVA) = √3 · V(kV) · I(kA)**.
- **Rated making current** = peak of first current loop ≈ **2.55 × symmetrical breaking current** at 50 Hz (includes DC offset, 1.8√2 = 2.55).
- **Short-time current**: the rms current the breaker carries for 1 s or 3 s.
- **Rated operating duty (IEC)**: O − 0.3 s − CO − 3 min − CO (or O − 3 min − CO − 3 min − CO). Autoreclose duty: O − 0.3 s − CO − 3 min − CO.
- **Fault MVA** = Base MVA / X_pu (pu reactance up to the fault).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Grid fault level 2000 MVA at 11 kV: I = 2000/(√3 × 11) = 2000/19.053 = **104.97 kA**. Rated breaker must be ≥ that (a 40 kA breaker is inadequate; fault limiting reactors or a 125 kA class would be needed).

**Example 2.** A breaker rated 25 kA (symmetrical), 11 kV: breaking capacity = 1.732 × 11 × 25 = **476.3 MVA**; making capacity = 2.55 × 25 = **63.75 kA peak**.

**Example 3.** Base 100 MVA, source reactance 0.05 pu: fault MVA = 100/0.05 = 2000 MVA (as above).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the 11 kV nominal voltage when the ratings table uses rated voltage 12 kV; use the actual system voltage for a fault MVA to current conversion.
- Forgetting √3 in the three-phase MVA formula.
- Quoting making current as rms: it is a peak value.
- Choosing breaker on normal current alone, ignoring fault level.

lessons.title: Oil circuit breakers: bulk oil and minimum oil

scenes.text: In a 1960s 33 kV substation, a breaker is a steel tank of insulating oil with three contacts dipping into it.
When it trips, the arc vaporises the oil into a hydrogen-rich gas bubble that cools and quenches the arc.

steps.title: Principle and construction
steps.body:
The arc decomposes transformer oil into about **70 % hydrogen** (high thermal conductivity, strong cooling) plus acetylene, methane and carbon; the gas bubble around the arc and the oil turbulence deionise the path.

**Bulk oil CB (BOCB)**: contacts in an earthed steel tank (dead tank) full of oil; the oil serves for both arc quenching and insulation to earth. Types: plain break (simple), and arc-control (explosion pot) type in which the arc is forced through a small pot with vents so that pressure builds and oil is blasted across the arc (axial or cross blast).
**Minimum oil CB (MOCB)**: arc is confined in an insulating (porcelain/FRP) interrupting chamber at line potential (live tank); only about 10 % of the oil volume is used, and insulation to earth is by porcelain/air.
**Maintenance**: oil carbonises and must be filtered or replaced after a number of fault interruptions.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Oil needed for insulation: in BOCB the oil acts as insulation, so volume is large (hundreds of litres at 33 kV); in MOCB the oil is only in the chamber (tens of litres). Hence MOCB is lighter and has a smaller fire risk.

**Example 2.** Oil test: before use, insulating oil must withstand a breakdown voltage (BDV) test of at least about 30 kV across a 2.5 mm gap (typical acceptance limit; check the relevant standard). Carbonised oil after several fault clearances falls below this and must be filtered, which is why BOCB maintenance is heavy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying oil quenches the arc because of its dielectric strength alone; the key is hydrogen and the pressure blast.
- Saying MOCB is a dead-tank design; it is a live-tank design.
- Ignoring fire/explosion hazards and the need for oil testing (BDV).

lessons.title: Air circuit breakers: air-break and air-blast

scenes.text: At a 400 kV station an air-blast breaker trips with a thunderous bang as a jet of compressed air slams the arc.
Inside a 415 V panel, a smaller air circuit breaker just uses an arc chute.

steps.title: Two families
steps.body:
**Air-break (ACB)**: operates in free air at atmospheric pressure. The arc is lengthened by magnetic blowout coils and forced into **arc chutes** with metal splitter plates which cool and split it (high-resistance interruption). Used for LV (up to 1 kV) and medium voltage up to about 15 kV.
**Air-blast (ABCB)**: compressed air at about **20–30 kg/cm² (≈ 2–3 MPa)** is blown across or along the arc. Blast types: axial blast (air along arc), cross blast, radial blast. Merits: fast, no fire hazard, repeated duty, arcing time ~ half a cycle. Demerits: need for a compressor plant, air leakage, high RRRV sensitivity requiring a shunt resistor, noise and chopping overvoltage. Large ABCBs were used at 245–765 kV until replaced by SF₆.
Air-blast breakers use a separate isolating blade that opens after the blast to give a visible gap.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** An ACB arc chute has splitter plates each giving about a 25 V near-electrode drop. To interrupt on a 415 V system the total arc voltage must exceed the peak driving voltage 415 × √2 = 587 V, so the plates needed = 587/25 = 23.5, i.e. at least **24 plates** (designs use more for margin).

**Example 2.** Compressed air at 25 kg/cm² = 25 × 0.0980665 = 2.45 MPa (≈ 24.5 bar).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that air-blast breakers need a compressor plant, receivers and dehydrators.
- Confusing kg/cm² and bar (1 kg/cm² ≈ 0.98 bar).
- Thinking air-break breakers use compressed air: they use free air and arc chutes.

lessons.title: SF₆ circuit breakers

story.title: Why the grid switched to a heavy gas

scenes.text: Sulphur hexafluoride is five times heavier than air, colourless, odourless and non-flammable.
It is a superb insulator and arc quencher, but also a very potent greenhouse gas.

steps.title: Properties and types
steps.body:
**Properties**: electronegative (captures free electrons and forms heavy negative ions, so the arc cools very quickly); dielectric strength about 2.5 times that of air at the same pressure and rises with pressure; non-toxic, inert and non-flammable when pure; the arc products (low sulphur fluorides, HF) are toxic and are absorbed by alumina/molecular sieve filters. GWP ≈ 23 500 times CO₂ (100-year), so leakage control matters.
**Types**: (1) **Double pressure** (obsolete): high-pressure reservoir plus low-pressure tank; (2) **Single pressure puffer**: a piston/cylinder attached to the moving contact compresses the gas (pressure ≈ 5–6 bar at filling) and blasts it through the nozzle on opening; (3) **Self-blast / thermal-expansion** and **rotating-arc** interrupters, which use the arc's own energy and need low operating energy. Operating mechanisms: spring, hydraulic or spring-hydraulic.
**Uses**: 33 kV to 800 kV AIS, and GIS (gas-insulated switchgear) in compact urban substations.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Air has a breakdown strength of about 3 MV/m (30 kV/cm) for uniform field. For a withstand of 100 kV peak the gap in air = 100 000/3 × 10⁶ = 33.3 mm. SF₆ (2.5×) : 13.3 mm — a much smaller gap, hence compact GIS.

**Example 2.** Gas density: SF₆ molar mass 146 g/mol vs air 29 g/mol, ratio 146/29 = 5.0 — SF₆ is about five times heavier than air, so leaks collect in cable trenches and basements (asphyxiation risk in low areas).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing SF₆ is toxic when pure; the by-products after arcing are the hazard.
- Forgetting to monitor gas density (not just pressure) with temperature compensation.
- Confusing puffer (mechanical compression) with self-blast (arc-energy) designs.

lessons.title: Lab: Vacuum circuit breakers and energy in the arc

story.title: The 11 kV panel that never needs oil

scenes.text: A sealed bottle holds contacts in a vacuum of 10⁻⁶ torr or better.
The arc is only metal vapour from the contacts and vanishes within a few microseconds of current zero.

steps.title: Principle and features
steps.body:
In a vacuum interrupter (pressure ≈ 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁸ torr) there is no gas to ionise. On opening, a **metal-vapour arc** forms from the cathode spots. At current zero the vapour condenses on the contacts and shield within microseconds, so the **dielectric strength recovers extremely fast** (about 20 kV/µs).
- Arc voltage is only ~20–30 V, so arc energy is tiny; contact erosion is small ⇒ long life (10⁴–10⁵ operations; electrical life 30+ fault interruptions).
- Contacts: butt contacts of **Cu–Cr** (low chopping current ~ 3–5 A, good dielectric strength) with spiral or axial magnetic-field designs to keep the arc diffuse.
- Metal bellows allow contact travel (~ 8–10 mm at 11 kV) without air leakage; ceramic envelope.
- Used 3.3–33 kV (some 38–72 kV) for distribution, motors, furnaces, capacitor banks. **Demerits**: chopping overvoltages (use arresters/snubbers), loss of vacuum is hard to detect (use a high-voltage test of the bottle).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Arc energy in a vacuum interrupter: V_arc = 20 V, current i = Ip sin ωt with Irms = 25 kA (Ip = 35.36 kA), last half-loop: ∫ i dt = 2Ip/ω = 2 × 35 355/314.16 = 225.1 C. Energy = 20 × 225.1 = **4.50 kJ**.

**Example 2.** An air-break breaker with 1000 V arc voltage for the same current has energy 1000 × 225.1 = 225 kJ — 50 times more heat to dissipate, explaining the long life of vacuum breakers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the arc can't form in a vacuum; it forms in metal vapour.
- Using rms current for the ∫ i dt step: use the peak value with 2Ip/ω.
- Assuming vacuum breakers have no overvoltage issues; chopping is real.

steps.title: Selection guide
steps.body:
- **LV (≤ 1 kV)**: air circuit breaker (ACB) up to 6300 A, MCCB, MCB.
- **MV 3.3–33 kV**: vacuum breaker (default); SF₆ also used; minimum oil only in legacy.
- **HV/EHV 66–800 kV**: SF₆ puffer / self-blast; GIS where land is scarce, polluted or coastal.

- **Capacitor banks**: restrike-free vacuum or SF₆ with pre-insertion/controlled switching.

lessons.title: Fuses: terms, characteristics and HRC fuse

scenes.text: A mixer grinder shorts out and a small ceramic cartridge in the main board sacrifices itself.
That fuse has just prevented a cable fire and a trip of the upstream breaker.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A fuse is a thin conductor that melts when current exceeds its rating for long enough, breaking the circuit.
- **Current rating**: the rms current the fuse carries continuously without melting or deterioration.
- **Fusing current**: minimum current at which the element melts (in a specified time, e.g. 4 h or conventional time).
- **Fusing factor** = minimum fusing current / current rating (always > 1; for rewirable fuses 1.4–1.7; for HRC 1.1–1.5 typical).
- **Prospective current**: the rms of the symmetrical fault current that would flow if the fuse were replaced by a link.
- **Cut-off current**: maximum instantaneous current reached before the fuse clears (the fuse is current limiting).
- **Pre-arcing time** + **arcing time** = **total operating time**. **I²t (Joule integral)**: let-through energy; ∫ i² dt.
**HRC (high rupturing capacity) fuse**: silver or copper element(s) with notches, enclosed in a ceramic body packed with quartz sand. The arc melts the sand into fulgurite, which absorbs energy and raises arc resistance. It is current limiting and has a breaking capacity up to 80–120 kA. Merits: fast, no maintenance, cheap. Demerits: must be replaced after operation, discrimination only by I²t, ageing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 20 A rated fuse melts at 30 A: fusing factor = 30/20 = **1.5**.

**Example 2.** Prospective fault current 50 kA but cut-off at 8 kA: the circuit sees 16% of the peak, so mechanical stress on cables and busbars (∝ i²) falls to (8/50)² = 0.0256 — about 2.6 % of the unlimited value. For a cut-off, the maximum let-through for a 100 A fuse at 50 kA is read from manufacturer cut-off curves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Fusing factor below 1 (impossible).
- Saying the fuse operates on voltage.
- Replacing a blown fuse with a higher-rated one or a wire.

Fusing current depends on diameter as d^1.5, not d².

steps.title: Law and time-current
steps.body:
Heat generated I²R is proportional to I²·(ρl/ (π d²/4)) ∝ I²/d²; heat lost from the surface ∝ π d l. At equilibrium I² /d² ∝ d ⇒ **I ∝ d^(3/2)** (Preece's law, I = k d^1.5, k depends on the metal).
So I₂/I₁ = (d₂/d₁)^1.5.
The **time–current characteristic** is inverse (I²t ≈ constant at high currents). **Discrimination (grading)** between two fuses in series: the total I²t of the downstream fuse must be less than the pre-arcing I²t of the upstream fuse. Typical rule: current rating ratio ≥ 1.6 for HRC fuses of the same make.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A wire of 0.2 mm fuses at 5 A. For 0.4 mm: I = 5 × (0.4/0.2)^1.5 = 5 × 2.828 = **14.14 A**.

**Example 2.** Diameter needed for 20 A if 0.2 mm fuses at 5 A: (d/0.2) = (20/5)^(2/3) = 4^0.6667 = 2.52 ⇒ d = **0.504 mm**.

**Example 3.** Fuse at I = 50 A clears in 0.01 s: I²t = 2500 × 0.01 = 25 A²s. At 100 A the time falls to 25/10 000 = 2.5 ms (in the I²t = constant region).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d² instead of d^1.5 for the current-diameter law.
- Using the I²t constancy at low overloads, where heat loss makes the curve flat.
- Giving the same rating to upstream and downstream fuses (no discrimination).

story.title: Never open an isolator on load

steps.title: Equipment
steps.body:
- **Isolator (disconnector)**: opens a circuit under no load (only negligible charging or voltage-transformer current) to give a visible gap for safety. It has no arc-quenching capability. **Interlock** it with the breaker.
- **Earthing switch**: grounds an isolated circuit to discharge stored charge and protect personnel.
- **Load-break switch**: can make and break normal load current but not fault current; with HRC fuses it forms a fuse-switch.
- **Contactor**: remote-controlled switch for frequent operation (millions of cycles), AC1–AC4 duty categories; does not clear faults itself.
**Switching sequence**: *Opening*: open the circuit breaker, then the isolator(s) (load side then bus side), then close the earth switch. *Closing*: remove earth, close isolators, then close the breaker.
**Bus schemes**: single busbar (cheap, outage on bus fault), sectionalised bus, main-and-transfer (bypass any breaker), double busbar (flexible), **breaker-and-a-half** (3 breakers for 2 circuits ⇒ 1.5 CB/circuit; very reliable), **ring bus** (n breakers for n circuits).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A breaker-and-a-half bay with 8 feeders: breakers = 1.5 × 8 = **12**. A ring bus with 8 circuits: 8 breakers. A double breaker scheme: 2 × 8 = 16.

**Example 2.** Isolating a transformer feeder: (1) open CB; (2) open load-side isolator; (3) open bus-side isolator; (4) close earth switches; (5) issue the permit to work.

steps.title: LV devices
steps.body:
**MCB**: thermal (bimetal) element for overload and magnetic (solenoid) for short circuit. Tripping curves (instantaneous trip range): **B: 3–5 × In** (resistive, lighting), **C: 5–10 × In** (general, small motors), **D: 10–20 × In** (transformers, high inrush). Breaking capacity 3–10 kA (to 25 kA).
**MCCB**: up to 1600 A with adjustable thermal and magnetic trips (Ir, Isd, Ii), breaking capacity up to 100 kA+.
**RCCB/RCD**: measures the vector sum of phase and neutral currents in a toroid; trips if residual current I∆n is exceeded (trip between 0.5 and 1 × I∆n). **30 mA** for protection against electric shock; 100–300 mA for fire protection; no overload protection, so combine with MCB (RCBO). **ELCB (voltage type)** is obsolete.

steps.title: Method

steps.title: Requirements and zones
steps.body:
**Fundamental requirements**: **selectivity** (discrimination: trip only the faulted section), **speed**, **sensitivity** (detect minimum fault), **reliability** (dependability + security), **stability** (no trip on through faults or inrush), simplicity and economy.
**Zones of protection** overlap around circuit breakers so no equipment is unprotected: generator, transformer, bus, line, motor each have a zone. **Primary protection** acts in its zone; **backup protection** (remote or local) acts if the primary fails, with a time delay.
**Terms**: pick-up (the minimum actuating quantity), reset/drop-off ratio, operating time, reach, burden (VA), overshoot time, relay characteristic.
**Instrument transformers**: **CT** (secondary 1 A or 5 A; series connection; secondary must never be open – dangerous voltage); accuracy class 5P10/10P20 for protection (error 5 %, accuracy limit factor 10); **PT/CVT** (110 V line to line secondary).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** CT ratio 600/5 and primary current 1500 A: secondary current = 1500 × 5/600 = **12.5 A**.

**Example 2.** CT 5P20 with burden 15 VA, 5 A secondary: accuracy limit current = 20 × 5 = 100 A secondary; i.e. the CT keeps its 5 % composite error up to 20 × rated current (3000 A primary for 600/5). Faults above that cause saturation, so the relay may under-measure.

**Example 3.** PT ratio 11 kV/110 V = 100:1. Line voltage 10.8 kV gives 108 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Opening a CT secondary while the primary is energised.
- Confusing sensitivity (minimum detectable fault) with selectivity.
- Using a measurement-class CT for protection; it saturates early.

story.title: A disc that spins to protect

scenes.text: Inside an old over-current relay a metal disc rotates faster as current rises, like a miniature energy meter.
Higher current ⇒ more torque ⇒ shorter operating time: that is the inverse characteristic.

steps.title: Constructions
steps.body:
**Attracted armature** (instantaneous): plunger, hinged armature or balanced beam; force ∝ I² so it works on AC and DC; very fast (≈ 10–50 ms); high-set instantaneous element.
**Induction type**: two fluxes φ₁ and φ₂ with phase difference α induce eddy currents in a disc or cup; torque **T ∝ φ₁φ₂ sin α**. Constructions: **shaded-pole** (copper ring delays one part of flux), **watt-hour/double-winding** and **induction cup** (high speed, used for directional units). Disc travel gives time delay; a permanent drag magnet limits speed and a spiral spring provides restraint. Time-setting multiplier (TMS) changes the disc travel distance; the plug-setting bridge tap-selects current pick-up.
**Directional relay**: torque **T = K V I cos(φ − τ)**, where τ is the maximum-torque angle; operates for power flow in the trip direction. A voltage polarising quantity is needed (e.g. 90° connection with quadrature voltage).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** If operating current doubles in an induction disc, flux φ₁ and φ₂ both ∝ I (before saturation), so torque ∝ I²: four times, so speed is higher and time shortens (inverse time with a definite minimum when the iron saturates).

**Example 2.** Directional relay with τ = 45° and current lagging voltage by 60°: cos(60° − 45°) = cos 15° = 0.966 ⇒ about 97 % of maximum torque, so it operates strongly.

**Example 3.** At φ = τ + 90° = 135° torque = K V I cos 90° = 0 ⇒ the relay restrains.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying induction relays work on DC; they need AC.
- Confusing TMS (time) and PS (pick-up current).
- Forgetting that a directional relay needs a voltage reference.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
**Plug-setting multiplier PSM = fault current in relay coil / (rated secondary current × plug setting)** = I_f / (CT ratio × PS × In).
Relay current = I_f / CT ratio.
**IEC inverse characteristics**: t = TMS × k / (PSM^α − 1)
- Standard (normal) inverse: k = 0.14, α = 0.02
- Very inverse: k = 13.5, α = 1
- Extremely inverse: k = 80, α = 2
- Long-time inverse: k = 120, α = 1
Plug setting typically 50–200 % in steps of 25 %; the pick-up should be 1.1–1.3 × maximum load current; TMS 0.05–1.0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the CT ratio when computing PSM.
- Using PS as a pick-up in primary amperes: PS is a percentage of relay rated current.
- Setting pick-up below the maximum load (nuisance trip).

lessons.title: Lab: Time grading, directional and earth-fault protection

scenes.text: A radial 11 kV feeder has relays at the incoming, mid and end switchboards.
The farthest relay must be fastest; each upstream relay waits a grading margin.

steps.title: Grading
steps.body:
**Time grading** on a radial feeder: the relay nearest the fault operates first; each upstream relay is delayed by a **discrimination (grading) margin** of ≈ 0.3–0.5 s covering breaker opening time (~0.1 s), relay overshoot (~0.05 s), errors (~0.1 s) and a safety margin. Use TMS and PS together; start from the farthest relay with the lowest TMS (e.g. 0.05–0.1).
**Ring mains / parallel feeders**: directional relays (looking away from the source) with grading in each direction avoid sympathetic tripping.
**Earth-fault protection**: residual connection of three CTs (sum of phase currents = 3I₀) with lower pick-up (10–40 %); core-balance CT (zero-sequence CT) for cables; restricted earth fault (REF) for transformer and generator windings; sensitive earth-fault for high-impedance earthing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Relay B (downstream) operates in 0.5 s at the fault. With a 0.4 s margin relay A (upstream) must operate in **0.9 s**; for PSM 8 (normal inverse factor 3.297 s) TMS = 0.9/3.297 = 0.273.

**Example 2.** The same example, relay B at 0.4 s and margin 0.4 s ⇒ relay A at 0.8 s ⇒ TMS = 0.8/3.297 = **0.243**.

**Example 3.** Residual earth-fault: with a balanced load of 300 A per phase the three CT secondaries sum to zero, so an earth-fault relay can be set at 10 % of the CT rating (e.g. 40 A on 400/5) without nuisance trips. An earth fault of 200 A on one phase leaves a residual of 200 A on the primary, i.e. 200/80 = 2.5 A in the relay (50 % of 5 A) ⇒ it operates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Grading without including the breaker operating time.
- Setting earth-fault pick-up above the minimum earth-fault current.
- Applying non-directional relays on parallel feeders.

steps.title: Evolution
steps.body:
**Static relays**: analog electronics (comparators, op-amps) – no moving parts, low burden (< 1 VA), fast, flexible characteristics. **Digital**: microprocessor with A/D converter. **Numerical**: DSP-based, sampling, digital filtering (e.g. DFT/Fourier), multifunction (over-current, earth fault, thermal, breaker-fail, auto-reclose), disturbance recorder, communication (IEC 61850, DNP3), self-supervision, settings groups.
**Sampling**: an anti-alias low-pass filter must remove frequencies above fs/2 (Nyquist). With 32 samples per cycle at 50 Hz, fs = 1600 Hz ⇒ Nyquist 800 Hz.
**Merits**: low burden, adaptive settings, event records. **Demerits**: need auxiliary DC, EMI/cyber issues, software versions.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Sampling 16 samples/cycle at 50 Hz: fs = 800 Hz; Nyquist = **400 Hz**; the 9th harmonic (450 Hz) would alias.

**Example 2.** Capstone: a 400/5 CT feeder carries 280 A max. Set PS: relay load current = 280/80 = 3.5 A = 70 % of 5 A. Take pick-up 1.25 × load = 4.375 A ⇒ choose PS = 100 % (5 A, equal to 400 A primary) for margin. Check the minimum fault 1200 A: PSM = 1200/400 = 3 (> 1.5 sensitivity). Dependable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sampling without an anti-alias filter.
- Assuming digital relays make CT saturation irrelevant.
- Not recording the setting version after changes.

lessons.title: Transformer protection: Buchholz and differential

story.title: The bubble that warned of a fault

scenes.text: In a 20 MVA transformer a loose connection arcs slowly under oil, releasing gas.
The gas collects in the Buchholz relay and rings an alarm days before a failure.

steps.title: Schemes
steps.body:
**Buchholz relay** (gas-operated, between tank and conservator, ≥ 500 kVA): *alarm* on slow gas accumulation from incipient faults; *trip* on a surge of oil (severe internal fault). Also: oil/winding temperature, pressure-relief valve, over-flux (V/Hz) relay.
**Differential protection (Merz–Price)**: compares currents entering and leaving. Corrections: (1) **CT ratio matching** so secondary currents are equal under load; (2) **phase-shift compensation**: CTs on the star side connect in delta and CTs on the delta side connect in star (for Dy transformer); (3) **zero-sequence filtering**; (4) **biased (percentage) differential** to prevent maladjustment on through faults due to tap changers and CT errors; (5) **harmonic restraint**: 2nd harmonic (≈ 15–20 %) blocks inrush, 5th harmonic blocks over-excitation.
**Biased characteristic**: operating current Id = |I₁ − I₂|, restraint current Ir = (I₁ + I₂)/2; trips if Id > slope × Ir + minimum pick-up (slope 20–40 %).
**REF**: restricted earth fault on the earthed-star winding; **over-current + earth-fault** as backup.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 10 MVA, 33/11 kV Dy11: HV rated current = 10 000/(√3 × 33) = **174.95 A**; LV = 10 000/(√3 × 11) = **524.86 A**. With HV CTs (star) of ratio N₁ and LV CTs (delta) of ratio N₂, balance requires 174.95/N₁ = √3 × 524.86/N₂ ⇒ N₂/N₁ = 909.1/174.95 = **5.196** (= 3√3).

**Example 2.** Slope 25 %: I₁ = 5 A, I₂ = 4 A ⇒ Id = 1, Ir = 4.5 ⇒ 22 % < 25 % ⇒ **restrain**. I₁ = 5 A, I₂ = 3 A ⇒ Id = 2, Ir = 4 ⇒ 50 % ⇒ **trip**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Connecting CTs wrongly (delta on delta) so the relay trips on healthy load.
- Ignoring tap-changer range when selecting the slope.
- Tripping on inrush due to missing 2nd-harmonic restraint.

lessons.title: Generator and motor protection

scenes.text: A 200 MW unit trips on loss of excitation within 2 seconds.
A stator earth-fault relay and negative-sequence relay both saved the machine in earlier events.

steps.title: Generator
steps.body:
- **Stator differential** (percentage) for phase faults; **inter-turn** protection via split-phase or V.T. residual.
- **Stator earth fault**: neutral earthed through resistor/transformer limits current; a relay at the neutral covers about **95 %** of winding (the last 5 % near the neutral has too little voltage); the **100 %** scheme adds a 3rd harmonic or sub-harmonic injection scheme. A fault at x p.u. from neutral gives current ∝ x; unprotected fraction = pick-up/maximum current.
- **Rotor earth fault** (DC injection); **loss of excitation** (impedance/mho relay); **reverse power** (motoring, turbine protection); **negative-sequence** (rotor heating, I₂²t = K); over-/under-frequency and voltage; out-of-step; over-flux; back-up impedance.
**Motor**: thermal overload (replica of I²R heating), short-circuit (instantaneous), locked rotor/stall, **single-phasing** (negative-sequence or phase-failure relay), under-voltage, earth fault, RTD winding temperature, and number of starts per hour limit.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Alternator neutral earthing resistor limits full-voltage earth fault current to 200 A. Relay pick-up 20 A ⇒ unprotected winding = 20/200 = **10 %**; reduce by lowering the pick-up to 10 A ⇒ 5 %.

**Example 2.** Generator capability I₂²t = K = 10 s (I₂ in per unit). With I₂ = 0.2 pu the time to damage is t = 10/0.2² = 10/0.04 = **250 s**; with 0.5 pu: 40 s.

**Example 3.** Motor 100 kW, 415 V draws 175 A; starting 6 × FLC = 1050 A for 8 s; thermal relay must allow 8 s at 6× (I²t ≈ 36 × 8 = 288 pu²·s) but trip a stall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing the neutral relay covers 100 % of the winding.
- Using only overload protection and ignoring single-phasing.
- Forgetting the cooling time restart limits.

lessons.title: Busbar protection and feeder protection (pilot, auto-reclose)

scenes.text: A flashover on a 220 kV bus must be cleared in under 100 ms or the system may lose stability.
Feeders use pilot wires or fibre to compare currents at both ends.

steps.title: Busbar and pilot protection
steps.body:
**Busbar protection**: current differential (sum of all feeder currents = 0 on a healthy bus). *High-impedance* scheme uses a stabilising resistor to stay stable when one CT saturates on an external fault; *low-impedance biased* scheme uses restraint currents and a check zone; *frame-leakage (earth-metal)* for metal-clad switchgear; interlocked back-up in MV.
**Pilot protection**: Merz–Price circulating-current and Translay (opposed-voltage) schemes, using pilot wires for short lines (≤ 10–15 km). **Carrier (PLC)** and **fibre-optic** differential for long lines; **phase-comparison** schemes.
**Auto-reclosing**: 80–90 % of overhead line faults are transient (arcs); the breaker is reclosed after a **dead time** (≈ 0.3–1 s single-phase, 0.5–1.5 s three-phase) to restore the line; one-shot or multiple-shot sequence; blocked for cable faults. **Single-pole tripping** improves stability on EHV lines.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Bus with 4 feeders carrying 300, 200, −350 and −150 A (in and out): sum = 0 ⇒ no operation. An internal fault adds 4 kA from sources: sum = 4 kA ⇒ trips.

**Example 2.** Auto-reclose dead time: de-ionisation of the arc channel requires t ≥ (kV/34.5 + 20) cycles (empirical rule for a three-phase reclose): for 132 kV, 132/34.5 + 20 = 23.8 cycles ≈ 0.48 s at 50 Hz.

**Example 3.** Pilot-wire line: the pilot loop resistance and capacitance limit the length. A 10 km pair of 5 Ω/km conductors has a loop resistance of 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 Ω, which already burdens the relay, so beyond about 10–15 km fibre or carrier is used.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Auto-reclosing on cable or transformer feeders (permanent faults).
- Using a low-impedance CT scheme without a check zone.
- Forgetting to block reclosure on a breaker-failure trip.

lessons.title: Lab: Distance (impedance) relays — reach on the secondary side

scenes.text: A distance relay computes V/I and compares with a set impedance proportional to the line length.
Zone 1 covers 80% of the line instantaneously; zone 2 and 3 provide remote backup.

steps.title: Principle and settings
steps.body:
The relay measures Z = V/I (apparent impedance seen) and operates when it falls inside its characteristic: **impedance** (circle centred at origin), **reactance**, **mho** (circle through the origin, inherently directional) or **quadrilateral**. Because the fault impedance ∝ distance, it is independent of source strength.
**Zones**: Zone 1 = 80–85 % of the protected line (instantaneous); Zone 2 = 100 % of the line + 50 % of the shortest adjacent line (0.3–0.4 s); Zone 3 = line + 100 % of the longest adjacent + 25 % (≈ 1 s).
**Secondary impedance**: Z_sec = Z_pri × (CT ratio)/(VT ratio).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 100 km line, 0.4 Ω/km ⇒ 40 Ω. Zone 1 = 0.8 × 40 = 32 Ω. CT 600/5 (120), VT 132 kV/110 V (1200): Z_sec = 32 × 120/1200 = **3.2 Ω**.

**Example 2.** Zone 2 with shortest adjacent 60 km: Z = 40 + 0.5 × (0.4 × 60) = 40 + 12 = **52 Ω primary**; secondary 5.2 Ω.

**Example 3.** Fault at 30 km: Z = 12 Ω primary — inside Zone 1 ⇒ instantaneous trip.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting Zone 1 at 100 % (overreach due to CT/VT and line errors).
- Forgetting arc resistance and infeed effect in Zone 2/3 reach.
- Mixing CT/VT ratio direction (Z_sec = Z_pri × CTR/VTR, not VTR/CTR).

steps.body:
**Aim**: to find the fusing current of wires of different diameters and verify I ∝ d^1.5, and to find the time–current characteristic of a cartridge fuse.
**Apparatus**: fuse holder, wires 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 mm, variable AC supply (autotransformer 0–250 V), ammeter, stopwatch.
**Procedure**: 1. Fit the wire; 2. raise the current slowly; note the current at which the wire melts; 3. repeat three times and average; 4. for the time characteristic apply fixed currents of 1.5×, 2×, 3× rating and note melting time; 5. plot I vs d on log–log paper (slope should be 1.5).

**Typical long questions (original style)**: (1) Derive the restriking voltage for L–C circuit and discuss RRRV. (2) Explain the working of an SF₆ puffer breaker. steps.title: Solved question
steps.body:
**Q.** 11 kV, 750 MVA fault level; find the breaking current and making current.
**A.** I = 750/(√3 × 11) = 750/19.05 = **39.4 kA**; making = 2.55 × 39.4 = **100.4 kA peak**. Select a 40 kA, 11/12 kV breaker (rated 12 kV, 40 kA, making 102 kA).

steps.body: Examiner: A 132 kV line trips on Zone 2 although the fault is at 90 % of the line. Why? Answer: Zone 1 reach is only 80 % to prevent overreach, so the last 20 % is cleared by Zone 2 with delay unless a communication-aided scheme (permissive overreach or pilot) is used.

items.q: Why must a CT secondary never be open?
items.a: With no secondary current to oppose the primary mmf, the flux saturates and a very high voltage is induced across the open secondary, endangering insulation and people.

items.q: Why is SF₆ better than air?
items.a: It is electronegative, has about 2.5 times the dielectric strength and cools and deionises the arc very fast.

items.q: Why is current chopping a problem?
items.a: The energy ½LI² in the load inductance converts to V = I√(L/C) across the capacitance, giving overvoltage that can damage windings.
It blocks differential tripping on magnetising inrush, which is rich in 2nd harmonic.
To avoid overreach from CT/VT errors and line parameter uncertainty.
